'''Enric Sala''' (born November 26, 1968) is a marine ecologist, author, and conservationist. He is known for his work in ocean conservation and his leadership of [[National Geographic Society]] Pristine Seas initiative.

== Early life and education ==
Sala was born in Girona, Catalonia, Spain on November 26, 1968. He grew up watching [[Jacques Cousteau]]'s shows<ref>{{Cite web |last=Sala |first=Enric |title=Enric Sala Instagram |url=https://www.instagram.com/p/CL2GfZfjfpl/ |url-status=live}}</ref> and dreamt of being a diver on the Cousteau's boat, the Calypso.<ref>{{Cite web |title=An Interview with National Geographic Fellow Enric Sala |url=https://blog.education.nationalgeographic.org/2008/11/18/an_interview_with_national_geographic_fellow_enric_sala/}}</ref> He earned a B.Sc. in biology from the [[University of Barcelona]] in 1991 and received a Ph.D. in ecology from the [[Aix-Marseille University]] in 1996.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Enric Sala, National Geographic Explorer-in-Residence and Author of The Nature of Nature |url=https://www.rewild.org/team/enric-sala |access-date=9 July 2026 |website=Re:Wild}}</ref>

== Career ==

Following his academic studies, Sala was a professor at [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] in La Jolla, California.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Explorer in Residence Enric Sala |url=https://explorers.nationalgeographic.org/directory/enric-sala |url-status=live |access-date=9 July 2026 |website=National Geographic Explorer Home}}</ref>

In 2006, Sala moved back to Spain to take on a newly created post as a marine conservation ecology researcher at the Spanish National Council for Scientific Research (CSIC).<ref>{{Cite web |title=One Earth: Enric Sala |url=https://www.oneearth.org/contributor/enric-sala/}}</ref> Sala eventually left academia, citing that he was "tired of writing the obituary of ocean life."<ref>{{Cite web |title=A Marine Ecologist Strives to Protect the Seas |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2016/01/03/travel/national-geographic-water-pollution.html |website=The New York Times}}</ref>

=== Pristine Seas ===
In 2008, Sala launched the Pristine Seas initiative with [[National Geographic Society]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Explorer in Residence Enric Sala |url=https://explorers.nationalgeographic.org/directory/enric-sala |url-status=live |access-date=9 July 2026 |website=National Geographic Explorer Home}}</ref> a project designed to document and advocate for the protection of marine environments. In 2011, he and filmmaker [[James Cameron]] were named National Geographic Explorers in Residence.<ref>{{Cite news |date=24 June 2011 |title=National Geographic names newest Explorers-in-Residence |url=https://www.mediaupdate.co.za/media/38609/national-geographic-names-newest-explorers-in-residence |url-status=live |access-date=9 July 2026 |work=Media Update}}</ref>

Pristine Seas has produced over 200 peer-reviewed scientific publications and 30 documentary films to inspire governments and the public to take action.<ref>{{Cite web |title=National Geographic Pristine Seas |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.org/explore/programs/pristine-seas |website=National Geographic Pristine Seas}}</ref> As of 2026, the project had conducted over 50 expeditions and has contributed to the establishment of 31 marine protected areas covering more than 6.9 million square kilometers.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Pristine Seas |url=https://www.nationalgeographic.org/society/our-programs/pristine-seas/ |url-status=live |access-date=9 July 2026 |website=National Geographic Society}}</ref> 

=== 30x30 ===
Sala was one of the principal architects of the [[30 by 30|30x30 movement]] to protect 30% of the land and sea by 2030. He was the lead author of a study published in ''Nature'' in 2021 that made the case for conserving the ocean for the benefit of biodiversity, food supply, and the climate.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Protecting the global ocean for biodiversity, food and climate |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-021-03371-z |website=Nature}}</ref> At the [[Convention on Biological Diversity|UN Biodiversity Conference]] in 2022, UN member states adopted the 30x30 target as part of the [[Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework]]. In 2025, he co-authored a study published in ''Marine Policy'' that outlined the pathway to protect 30% of the ocean by 2030.<ref>{{Cite web |title=A pathway to protect 30 % of coastal waters by 2030 |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0308597X25001885 |website=Marine Policy}}</ref>

=== Writing and film work ===
In 2020, Sala published ''The Nature of Nature: Why We Need the Wild'',<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Nature of Nature: Why We Need the Wild |url=https://books.google.com/books/about/The_Nature_of_Nature.html?id=iQ9QzAEACAAJ |website=Google Books}}</ref> a combination of memoir and science writing that makes the case for ocean conservation and tells the story of his transition from academia to advocacy. 

Sala has served as a producer on dozens of films about the ocean. The 2020 National Geographic Pristine Seas film ''The Last Ice''<ref>{{Cite web |title=The Last Ice |url=https://films.nationalgeographic.com/the-last-ice |website=National Geographic Documentary Films}}</ref> won an [[Emmy Awards|Emmy Award]] for Outstanding Nature Documentary. Sala is also an executive producer and science advisor of ''Ocean with David Attenborough'', a full-length feature film that released in May 2025. ''Ocean with David Attenborough'' won two [[Emmy Awards]], for Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program and Outstanding Sound Editing for a Nonfiction or Reality Program.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ocean with David Attenborough, co-produced by Revive Our Ocean, Wins Two Creative Arts Emmy® Awards |url=https://reviveourocean.org/news/ocean-with-david-attenborough-co-produced-by-revive-our-ocean-wins-two-creative-arts-emmy-awards/ |website=Revive Our Ocean}}</ref>

=== Scientific Research ===
Sala's research interests include marine ecology, specifically the study of human impact on ocean health and the effectiveness of no-take marine reserves.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Enric Sala |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?hl=en&user=SJuwAxYAAAAJ |url-status=live |access-date=9 July 2026 |website=Google Scholar}}</ref>

Notable findings from his research include:

* 2008 – Contributions to the identification of inverted biomass pyramids in coral reef ecosystems.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=27 February 2008 |title=Baselines and Degradation of Coral Reefs in the Northern Line Islands |url=https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0001548 |journal=[[PLOS One]]}}</ref>
* 2018 – Research on the economic viability of high-seas fishing, which concluded that a significant portion of current activity is dependent on government subsidies.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=6 June 2018 |title=The economics of fishing the high seas |url=https://www.science.org/doi/pdf/10.1126/sciadv.aat2504 |journal=[[Science Advances]]}}</ref>
* 2021 – Lead author on an international study identifying priority areas in the global ocean for the preservation of biodiversity, food, and climate regulation.<ref>{{Cite journal |date=15 April 2021 |title=Protecting the global ocean for biodiversity, food and climate |url=https://archimer.ifremer.fr/doc/00686/79809/82604.pdf |journal=[[Nature (journal)]]}}</ref>
